title: Area XIV review: Postflight Procedures
intro: One Task, twelve questions on teaching After Landing, Parking, and Securing: the shutdown flow, the postflight, writing up discrepancies and who may fix and sign them, passengers near a turning propeller, and airport security. Several follow a problem from earlier in the lesson flight to the tie-down.

questions.q: Halfway to the practice area on a dual lesson, the left fuel quantity gauge starts swinging between full and a quarter. Your learner, a private pilot, says she will pull its breaker and stick an INOP note on it so the lesson can go on under 91.213(d). What do you teach?
options: Do it now: deferring the gauge in flight under 91.213(d) lets the lesson go on, and maintenance hears about it at the next inspection
No deferral in flight: handle it with the AFM/POH procedures now, then after shutdown note it and report it to maintenance
Leave it alone and watch it: if it acts up again on the next lesson, that is the time to write it up for maintenance
Note it on her kneeboard and tell the next renter at the tie-down, since the pilot in command decides what is safe to fly
questions.why: Maintenance deferrals are not used for inflight discrepancies; the AFM/POH procedures are used in those situations [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]]. The 91.213(d) deferral she wants is the process for items found before flight. After the airplane is shut down, tied down and secured, squawks are noted and reported to maintenance [[24:349|AFH 17-15]], because the owner or operator, who has discrepancies repaired as Part 43 prescribes between inspections, can only fix what someone reports [[60:520|14 CFR 91.405(a)]]. Waiting to see if it happens again, or telling only the next renter, leaves maintenance out of the chain.

questions.q: Your student pilot owns the airplane she trains in. She shows you the PHAK line saying student, sport and recreational pilots may not do preventive maintenance, and asks whether she may clean and grease its wheel bearings herself after today's lesson. What do you teach?
options: The PHAK line settles it: she may neither do the job nor approve the work, and only a mechanic may service the bearings
She may do it and sign the entry, because a student pilot certificate is a Part 61 certificate and 43.3(g) excludes only sport pilots
She may do it and sign the entry once you endorse her logbook for that task, since 43.7(f) accepts an instructor endorsement
Teach the CFR: 43.3(g) excludes only sport pilots, but 43.7(f) needs at least a private certificate to approve the return to service
questions.why: Servicing landing gear wheel bearings, such as cleaning and greasing, is on the Appendix A(c) list [[60:142|14 CFR Part 43 App. A(c)]]. A student pilot certificate is one of the Part 61 pilot certificates [[60:194|14 CFR 61.5(a)(1)]], and 43.3(g) excludes only holders of a sport pilot certificate [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(g)]]. The PHAK line [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]] does not match that text, and the CFR governs. But only a person holding at least a private pilot certificate may approve an aircraft for return to service after preventive maintenance [[60:132|14 CFR 43.7(f)]], and no one may fly it until it is approved and the entry is made [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(a)]]. That is the trap in the second option: doing the work and signing it off are separate rules. No rule lets an instructor endorsement replace the certificate. In practice, teach her to write it up and leave the job to someone who can sign for it.

questions.q: After a night lesson, your learner, a private pilot who co-owns the airplane, replaces a cracked position light lens and makes a 43.9 entry with his signature, certificate number and kind of certificate. He says: "My signature returns the airplane to service, so the soft-brake squawk my partner wrote yesterday is covered too." What do you teach?
options: His signature approves the return to service only for the lens; the brake squawk still needs its own repair and its own entry
He is right: a complete 43.9 entry signed by a private pilot approves the whole airplane for return to service until the next inspection
His entry approves nothing until a mechanic countersigns it, since pilots may do preventive maintenance but may not approve it
He is right only if he also checked the brakes, since an entry covers whatever the signer inspected on the same day
questions.why: Replacing lenses of position lights is on the Part 43 Appendix A(c) list [[60:142|14 CFR Part 43 App. A(c)]], and a private pilot may approve the return to service after doing it [[60:132|14 CFR 43.7(f)]], so no countersignature is needed. But the signature constitutes the approval for return to service only for the work performed [[60:132|14 CFR 43.9(a)]]. The brake squawk stays open until the owner or operator has it repaired as Part 43 prescribes [[60:520|14 CFR 91.405(a)]], and the pilot in command still decides whether the airplane is in condition for safe flight [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7]].

questions.q: The landing light quit on final during the night part of a lesson. On the postflight your learner, a private pilot who owns the airplane and flies it under Part 91, finds the bulb good and traces the fault to a broken wire in the landing light circuit. What may she do?
options: Replace a bulb or lens if needed, but no wiring work, because Appendix A(c) lets a pilot troubleshoot no electrical circuit at all
Troubleshoot and repair it, and under the same item any broken circuit in the position or strobe light wiring as well
Troubleshoot and repair that circuit herself, since Appendix A(c) lists it for landing light wiring only, then make the entry
Nothing herself: because the light failed in flight, only certificated maintenance personnel may work on it afterward
questions.why: Appendix A(c) lists troubleshooting and repairing broken circuits in landing light wiring circuits as preventive maintenance, provided the job does not involve complex assembly operations [[60:142|14 CFR Part 43 App. A(c)]]. As an owner with a private certificate she may do it under 43.3(g) [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(g)]], approve the return to service [[60:132|14 CFR 43.7(f)]] and make the 43.9 entry [[60:132|14 CFR 43.9(a)]]. The limit is the tempting part: the wiring item names only landing light circuits, and for position lights the list allows only bulbs, reflectors and lenses. A failure in flight changes how it is handled in the air, with the AFM/POH procedures [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]], not who may fix it on the ground.

questions.q: Both magneto drops were normal on the runup. At shutdown the engine keeps running smoothly when your learner, a private pilot, turns the key to OFF for the grounding check, so she stops it with the mixture. She has the airplane again at 1400 and says, "It ran fine all flight, I will just recheck it then." What do you teach?
options: Rechecking at 1400 is right: if the engine dies at OFF then, the fault has cleared itself and no write-up is needed
She may fix it as preventive maintenance by reconnecting the magneto ground wire, then sign the entry before 1400
Write it up for a qualified AMT to check the system, and treat the propeller as live, since moving it could start the engine
With the key at OFF and the master OFF, no power reaches the magnetos, so the propeller is safe to handle until 1400
questions.why: The grounding check at idle tests the OFF position [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]; a normal runup does not test it. If the ground wire between the magneto and the switch is broken, the engine could start if the propeller is moved with residual fuel in a cylinder; stop it with the mixture, then have the system checked by a qualified AMT [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]]. A magneto needs no outside electrical power, so the master switch does not make the propeller safe [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]], and anyone touching a propeller should assume the ignition is on [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]. Rewiring the magneto ground is not on the Appendix A(c) list, so it is not a pilot job [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

questions.q: By her fifth lesson your learner reads the shutdown checklist aloud quickly and perfectly. Today her hand is on the mixture while she says "avionics off," and after the engine stops the avionics are still on. What is going on, and what do you coach?
options: The recital has come loose from the actions; have her touch each control, name it and give its reason, then confirm with the list
The method is the problem: the AFH says a shutdown checklist must be read and done one item at a time, never used to confirm a flow
Nothing serious: a fast, smooth recital shows the flow has become automatic, which is the point of overlearning this Task
Have her put the checklist away and shut down from memory, since reading it too fast is what caused the missed item
questions.why: The AIH warns that a verbal checklist can become so automatic that the recitation is decoupled from the thoughts and actions the items should trigger, so the pilot does not stop to consider each item [[25:79|AIH 3-28]]. The fix for a rushed recital is to touch, name and give the reason for each item. A checklist need not be a do-list: the actions can be done and then the checklist used to confirm them, so the second option is wrong; but pilots who drop the checklist and rely only on memory become complacent [[24:36|AFH 1-15]]. In the AFH list, avionics OFF comes before mixture IDLE CUTOFF [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].

questions.q: Your learner made a firm landing during today's pattern work. Her POH shutdown checklist has no ELT item. At the tie-down she asks whether she should listen on 121.5 MHz before shutting down, and when that applies. What do you teach?
options: Only after a firm or hard landing, since that is the one case in which the AIM asks pilots to check for an ELT signal
Only when ATC asks for it, since monitoring 121.5 MHz is an air traffic task and her POH checklist does not list it
Only on the last flight of the day, since one check after the final lesson covers every earlier flight in that airplane
Yes, today and at the end of every flight: the AIM asks for it before engine shutdown, so add it to her shutdown flow
questions.why: The AIM lists monitoring 121.5 MHz before engine shutdown at the end of each flight as a way to minimize false ELT alarms [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]]. It is not tied to a hard landing, to ATC or to the last flight of the day. When the POH shutdown checklist lacks the item, add it to the flow.

questions.q: A lesson ends with 12 gallons in tanks that hold 40 gallons. The airplane will sit for 10 days with no flight planned. What servicing does the AFH call for, and what weight change goes in the write-up for the next pilot?
options: Leave the 12 gallons: fuel is added only for a planned flight, so the next pilot fuels to that flight's needs
Fill the tanks to prevent condensation: 28 gallons, adding 168 pounds the next pilot's weight and balance must include
Fill the tanks to prevent condensation: 40 gallons, adding 240 pounds the next pilot's weight and balance must include
Fill the tanks to prevent condensation: 28 gallons, adding 196 pounds the next pilot's weight and balance must include
questions.why: If the airplane is going to be inactive, filling the tanks is good practice to prevent water condensation; fueling to a flight's planning requirements applies when another flight is planned [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]. Fuel added: 40 minus 12 is 28 gallons. Aviation gasoline weighs 6 pounds per gallon [[22:67|W&B Handbook 7-7]], so 28 x 6 = 168 pounds. Using the full 40 gallons counts fuel already aboard, and 7 pounds per gallon is not the avgas figure.

questions.q: In the climb on today's lesson, the turn coordinator's warning flag showed twice for a few seconds. Taxiing in across a busy ramp, your learner starts writing the squawk on her kneeboard while the airplane rolls. What do you coach?
options: Stop the airplane or hold the write-up until it is secured: on the ground she can stop, handle it, then resume taxi
Let her keep writing, since the AFH wants squawks written at once, before the details are lost during the shutdown
Let her keep writing but slow to a crawl, since a slow taxi leaves enough attention to both write and look outside
Take the airplane and write it yourself, since documenting discrepancies is the instructor's job and not the learner's
questions.why: On the ground the pilot has the option to stop the aircraft and resume taxi after addressing an issue [[30:47|RMH 6-4]]. Fixating on a minor failure displaces tasks of greater importance [[24:51|AFH 2-14]], and a crowded ramp is no place for it. The AFH has squawks noted and reported after the airplane is shut down, tied down and secured [[24:349|AFH 17-15]], not while it moves. Documenting discrepancies is the learner's part of the element (ACS AI.XIV.A.S3); take it over and she never learns it.

questions.q: Your school's Cessna has no MEL. A learner who has read AC 91-67A insists that because of it, every squawk must go in the aircraft maintenance records and any failure after takeoff must be repaired or deferred under the MEL before the next takeoff. What do you teach?
options: She is right: AC 91-67A sets those rules for every Part 91 airplane, MEL or not, so the school must follow them
No write-up is needed in an airplane without an MEL; telling the front desk at the end of the lesson is enough
Without an MEL nothing can be deferred, so every squawk grounds the airplane until a mechanic signs it off
Those rules are written for MEL operations; here the sources say note it and report it to maintenance, in the school's system
questions.why: The AC 91-67A rules she quotes sit in its chapter on conducting operations with an MEL: after-takeoff failures recorded in the maintenance records and fixed or deferred under the MEL before the next takeoff [[58:27|AC 91-67A 5.1.3]], and entries in the maintenance records or a discrepancy log [[58:28|AC 91-67A 5.2]]. For other airplanes the AFH says squawks are noted and reported to maintenance [[24:349|AFH 17-15]], and the sources name no format, so teach the school's system. A verbal report is not enough. Part 91 airplanes without an MEL can still defer under 91.213(d) [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]], with a rated pilot or mechanic deciding the item is not a hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(4)]].

questions.q: A lesson ends with a stop at the FBO to drop off your learner's friend, who rode in back. To save a restart, she plans to keep the engine idling while he climbs out and walks aft, then taxi on to the school's tie-down. What do you teach?
options: Fine if she briefs him to walk aft past the wing, away from the propeller, before he opens the door and steps out
Shut down first: the arc is nearly invisible, and people walking into it toward the cabin or tail have been hurt and killed
Fine if the rotating beacon is on, since the beacon tells him and the ramp workers that the engine is still running
Fine if the brakes are set and the throttle is at idle, the same steps the AFH uses before removing chocks near a running engine
questions.why: The propeller is nearly invisible, and the AFH records serious injuries and deaths of people walking or reaching into the arc to reach the cabin or move toward the tail [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]; that warning comes from its hand-propping section, and the same arc is beside the passenger's door. For a door opened with the propeller turning, the fix is to shut down first, and passengers move on the surface only as directed [[24:51|AFH 2-14]]. A brief does not stop the propeller, and the beacon program is voluntary, so a beacon is not a reliable sign of a running engine [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24]]. Idle power and set brakes do not stop the blade.

questions.q: At your home field, which has airline service, you watch your learner secure the airplane for the night while her two passengers wait. She pulls the tie-down chains drum-tight, installs the control lock and the pitot and cowling covers, and sends the passengers ahead to the terminal through a gate onto the fenced airline boarding ramp. What do you debrief as errors?
options: Only the lock and covers: with the chains that tight, the tie-downs alone hold the airplane and keep the controls still
Only the passengers: the chains are right, since the AFH wants chains pulled tight so the airplane cannot move at all
The chains and the passengers: chains need some slack, and passengers need an escort and must stay out of the SIDA
The covers and the passengers: covers are for hangared airplanes, and passengers need an escort and must stay out of the SIDA
questions.why: Chains are not flexible, so they are not made taut; the airplane keeps some movement and the airframe is not damaged. The AFH has the flight controls secured on a tied-down airplane and suggests pitot tube and cowling inlet covers [[24:60|AFH 2-23]], so those were right. Passengers not under the pilot's direct supervision need an escort for safety and ramp security [[24:51|AFH 2-14]]. A Secured Area, where airline passengers board, is always a SIDA, and entry without authorization and displayed ID is prohibited [[33:173|AIM 2-3-15]]; people seen entering without proper ID may be reported to TSA and face fines and prosecution, so brief passengers [[33:174|AIM 2-3-15]].
